claim: IR56d is an ionotropic receptor required for hexanoic acid taste in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, taste neurons expressing the ionotropic receptor 56d (IR56d) are required for reflexive behavioral responses to the medium-chain fatty acid, hexanoic acid.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Ahn et al., 2017; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2018).

claim: Flies can discriminate medium-chain fatty acids from both short- and long-chain fatty acids.
source: Our results indicate that flies are able to discriminate medium-chain fatty acids from both short- and long-chain fatty acids, but not from other medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from aversive taste memory assays shown in Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Flies cannot discriminate between different medium-chain fatty acids.
source: Our results indicate that flies are able to discriminate medium-chain fatty acids from both short- and long-chain fatty acids, but not from other medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments in Figure 1F-H showing that aversive memory to one medium-chain fatty acid generalizes to other medium-chain fatty acids.

claim: IR56d neurons are broadly responsive to short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids.
source: While IR56d neurons are broadly responsive to short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids, genetic deletion of IR56d selectively disrupts response to medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating that IR56d neurons respond to fatty acids ranging from 4C to 10C.

claim: Genetic deletion of IR56d selectively disrupts response to medium-chain fatty acids.
source: While IR56d neurons are broadly responsive to short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids, genetic deletion of IR56d selectively disrupts response to medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 4G and calcium imaging data in Figure 5F showing that IR56dGAL4 mutants have reduced responses specifically to 6C, 7C, and 8C fatty acids.

claim: IR56d+ GR64f+ neurons are necessary for proboscis extension response (PER) to medium-chain fatty acids.
source: Further, IR56d+ GR64f+ neurons are necessary for proboscis extension response (PER) to medium-chain fatty acids, but both IR56d and GR64f neurons are dispensable for PER to short- and long-chain fatty acids, indicating the involvement of one or more other classes of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C and 3E showing that silencing either IR56d or GR64f neurons reduces PER to medium-chain fatty acids but not to short- or long-chain fatty acids.

claim: Both IR56d and GR64f neurons are dispensable for PER to short- and long-chain fatty acids.
source: Further, IR56d+ GR64f+ neurons are necessary for proboscis extension response (PER) to medium-chain fatty acids, but both IR56d and GR64f neurons are dispensable for PER to short- and long-chain fatty acids, indicating the involvement of one or more other classes of neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 3C and 3E showing no significant difference in PER to short- and long-chain fatty acids when IR56d or GR64f neurons are silenced.

claim: Discrimination of fatty acids occurs through differential receptor activation in shared populations of neurons.
source: Together, these findings reveal that IR56d is selectively required for medium-chain fatty acid taste, and discrimination of fatty acids occurs through differential receptor activation in shared populations of neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of behavioral discrimination data (Figure 1), calcium imaging showing broad responsiveness of IR56d neurons (Figure 5E), and selective loss of medium-chain fatty acid responses in IR56d mutants (Figure 5F).

claim: The taste system has the capacity to encode tastant identity within a taste category.
source: Our study uncovers a capacity for the taste system to encode tastant identity within a taste category.
evidence: This is supported by the discrimination experiments showing flies can distinguish between different classes of fatty acids (Figure 1B-D).

claim: Olfactory systems across phyla have enormous complexity in receptors and processing mechanisms that allow for detection and differentiation between odorants.
source: Across phyla, there is enormous complexity in olfactory receptors and downstream processing mechanisms that allow for detection and differentiation between odorants (Keller et al., 2017; Nara et al., 2011; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Taste coding is thought to be simpler than olfactory coding, with most animals possessing fewer taste receptors and a diminished ability to differentiate between tastants.
source: By contrast, taste coding is thought to be simpler, with most animals possessing fewer taste receptors and a diminished ability to differentiate between tastants (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015; Scott, 2018; Yarmolinsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IR56d is co-expressed with GR64f.
source: IR56d is co-expressed with GR64f (Ahn et al., 2017; Tauber et al., 2017), which broadly labels sweet GRNs (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Jiao et al., 2008; Slone et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by imaging data in Figure 6A-C showing colocalization.

claim: GR64f broadly labels sweet GRNs.
source: IR56d is co-expressed with GR64f (Ahn et al., 2017; Tauber et al., 2017), which broadly labels sweet GRNs (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Jiao et al., 2008; Slone et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IR56d-expressing GRNs are responsive to both sugars and fatty acids.
source: IR56d-expressing GRNs are responsive to both sugars and fatty acids, suggesting that these neurons may respond to diverse appetitive substances including multiple classes of fatty acids (Tauber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by calcium imaging data in Figure 5E showing responses to both sucrose and fatty acids.

claim: Flies can discriminate between sucrose (sugar) and hexanoic acid (fatty acid).
source: Conversely, we reported that flies can discriminate between sucrose (sugar) and hexanoic acid (fatty acid), revealing an ability to discriminate between appetitive stimuli of different modalities (Tauber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Flies trained with pairing of quinine and medium-chain hexanoic acid (6C) exhibited proboscis extension response (PER) to subsequent application of short-chain valeric acid (5C).
source: We found that flies that were trained with pairing of quinine and medium-chain hexanoic acid (6C) exhibited proboscis extension response (PER) to subsequent application of short-chain valeric acid (5C; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Aversive memory to 5C was not formed by training with 6C.
source: Thus, aversive memory to 5C was not formed by training with 6C, suggesting that flies can discriminate between these short- and medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 1B showing that trained flies still respond to 5C after training with 6C.

claim: Flies trained with 6C did not generalize aversive memory to 9C.
source: Similarly, flies trained with 6C did not generalize aversive memory to 9C, consistent with the idea that flies can also discriminate between medium- and long-chain fatty acids (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flies can discriminate between medium- and long-chain fatty acids.
source: Similarly, flies trained with 6C did not generalize aversive memory to 9C, consistent with the idea that flies can also discriminate between medium- and long-chain fatty acids (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 1C showing lack of generalization.

claim: Flies can form aversive taste memories to short-chain fatty acids.
source: To rule out the possibility that flies are unable to form aversive taste memories to short- and long-chain fatty acids, we trained with 5C and found robust aversive taste memory, which did not generalize to 9C (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Flies are capable of distinguishing between short-, medium-, and long-chain classes of fatty acids.
source: Together, these results suggest that flies are capable of distinguishing between short-, medium-, and long-chain classes of fatty acids.
evidence: This is supported by the combined behavioral data from Figure 1B-D showing discrimination between different classes.

claim: The aversive memory formed with 4C was generalized to 5C.
source: We found that the aversive memory formed with 4C was generalized to 5C, suggesting that flies cannot discriminate between different short-chain fatty acids (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Flies cannot discriminate between different short-chain fatty acids.
source: We found that the aversive memory formed with 4C was generalized to 5C, suggesting that flies cannot discriminate between different short-chain fatty acids (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 1E showing generalization of aversive memory.

claim: Flies formed aversive memories to 6C that generalized to 7C and 8C.
source: In both cases, flies formed aversive memories to 6C, and these generalized to 7C and 8C, suggesting that flies cannot discriminate between different medium chain fatty acids (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Flies cannot discriminate between different medium-chain fatty acids.
source: In both cases, flies formed aversive memories to 6C, and these generalized to 7C and 8C, suggesting that flies cannot discriminate between different medium chain fatty acids (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 1F and 1G showing generalization of aversive memory.

claim: Flies formed aversive memory to 7C that was generalized to 8C.
source: Again, flies formed aversive memory to 7C that was generalized to 8C (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The aversive memory formed with 10C was generalized to 9C.
source: We again found that the aversive memory formed with 10C was generalized to 9C, suggesting that flies cannot discriminate among long-chain fatty acids (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Flies cannot discriminate among long-chain fatty acids.
source: We again found that the aversive memory formed with 10C was generalized to 9C, suggesting that flies cannot discriminate among long-chain fatty acids (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 1I showing generalization of aversive memory.

claim: PER to consecutive applications of fatty acid shows no significant change in responsiveness over time.
source: We found that PER to consecutive applications of fatty acid shows no significant change in responsiveness over time, although in some cases PER to fatty acid trends downward (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of naïve groups across multiple experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Flies trained to 1% 6C could discriminate a different fatty acid tested at a different concentration (0.1%).
source: Even under these test conditions, flies remained able to discriminate between short- (5C) and medium-chain (6C) fatty acids as well as between long- (9C) and medium-chain (6C) fatty acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Despite a 10× difference in concentration, flies remain unable to distinguish between medium-chain fatty acids.
source: However, conditioning to a medium-chain fatty acid (6C) generalized to another medium-chain fatty acid (8C), suggesting that despite a 10× difference in concentration, flies remain unable to distinguish between medium-chain fatty acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Male flies respond to all fatty acids tested, though the overall responses were generally lower than those observed in females.
source: PER analysis with a panel of short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids revealed that males respond to all fatty acids tested, though the overall responses were generally lower than those observed in females (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Male flies are able to discriminate different classes of fatty acids, but are not able to distinguish fatty acids within the same class.
source: Therefore, male flies are also able to discriminate different classes of fatty acids, but are not able to distinguish fatty acids within the same class.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids have distinctly different olfactory activation profiles.
source: The short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids that we tested have distinctly different olfactory activation profiles (Hallem and Carlson, 2006), raising the possibility that flies can discriminate between these compounds using a combination of olfactory and gustatory information.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: All test groups were able to distinguish between sucrose and hexanoic acid after olfactory organ ablation.
source: All test groups were able to distinguish between sucrose and hexanoic acid, confirming that the ablation itself does not generally impact taste or memory formation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Flies trained to a medium-chain fatty acid (6C) did not generalize aversion to short- (5C) or long-chain (9C) fatty acids, regardless of the absence of one or both olfactory organs.
source: Further, flies trained to a medium-chain fatty acid (6C) did not generalize aversion to short- (5C) or long-chain (9C) fatty acids, regardless of the absence of one or both olfactory organs (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The taste system has the ability to encode the identity of different classes of fatty acids.
source: Taken together, our findings reveal an ability of the taste system to encode the identity of different classes of fatty acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the ablation experiments showing discrimination persists without olfactory input (Figure 2).

claim: Silencing IR56d-expressing neurons significantly reduced PER to the three medium-chain fatty acids (6C, 7C, and 8C).
source: Silencing IR56d-expressing neurons significantly reduced PER to the three medium-chain fatty acids (6C, 7C, and 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no difference in PER between control and IR56d-silenced flies in response to short-chain (4C and 5C) and long-chain (9C and 10C) fatty acids.
source: Conversely, there was no difference in PER between control and IR56d-silenced flies in response to short-chain (4C and 5C) and long-chain (9C and 10C) fatty acids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IR56d-expressing neurons are required for medium-chain fatty acid taste perception, but are dispensable for PER to both short- and long-chain fatty acids.
source: Therefore, IR56d-expressing neurons are required for medium-chain fatty acid taste perception, but are dispensable for PER to both short- and long-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 3C showing selective loss of PER to medium-chain fatty acids.

claim: Silencing GR64f-expressing neurons significantly reduced PER to sucrose.
source: In agreement with previous findings, silencing of GR64f-expressing neurons significantly reduced PER to sucrose (10 mM) as well as to medium-chain fatty acids (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Silencing GR64f-expressing neurons significantly reduced PER to medium-chain fatty acids.
source: In agreement with previous findings, silencing of GR64f-expressing neurons significantly reduced PER to sucrose (10 mM) as well as to medium-chain fatty acids (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There were no significant differences in responses to both short- and long-chain fatty acids between GR64f-silenced and control flies.
source: However, we found no significant differences in responses to both short- and long-chain fatty acids between GR64f-silenced (GR64f-GAL4 > UAS TNT) and control (GR64f-GAL4 > UAS impTNT) flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: PER elicited by short- and long-chain fatty acids is conferred by neurons that express neither IR56d nor GR64f.
source: Therefore, PER elicited by short- and long-chain fatty acids is conferred by neurons that express neither IR56d nor GR64f.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 3C and 3E showing that silencing either IR56d or GR64f neurons does not affect PER to short- and long-chain fatty acids.

claim: IR56dGAL4 labels labellar neurons that projected axons to both the taste peg and sweet taste regions of the SEZ.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we found GFP expression in labellar neurons that projected axons to both the taste peg and sweet taste regions of the SEZ (Figure 4B–E; Koh et al., 2014; Tauber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4B-E and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PER to sucrose did not differ between IR56dGAL4 and control flies.
source: In agreement with previous findings from genetic silencing of IR56d-expressing neurons, PER to sucrose did not differ between IR56dGAL4 and control flies (Figure 4F), suggesting that IR56dGAL4 is dispensable for response to sucrose.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PER to medium-chain fatty acids was disrupted in IR56dGAL4 flies (6C–8C), whereas PER to short- (4C and 5C) and long-chain fatty acids (9C and 10C) was not affected.
source: We found that PER to medium-chain fatty acids was disrupted in IR56dGAL4 flies (6C–8C), whereas PER to short- (4C and 5C) and long-chain fatty acids (9C and 10C) was not affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The observed decrease in PER to medium-chain fatty acids was rescued by transgenic expression of IR56d in the IR56dGAL4 mutant background.
source: The observed decrease in PER to medium-chain fatty acids was rescued by transgenic expression of IR56d in the IR56dGAL4 mutant background (IR56dGAL4;UAS-IR56d/+), confirming that the behavioral deficit of IR56dGAL4 flies is in fact due to loss of IR56d function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: IR56d appears to be selectively required for taste sensing of medium-chain fatty acids.
source: Therefore, IR56d appears to be selectively required for taste sensing of medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined behavioral and rescue data in Figure 4G.

claim: In flies heterozygous for IR56dGAL4, the labeled neurons were responsive to sucrose and all fatty acids tested, which ranged from 4C to 10C.
source: In flies heterozygous for IR56dGAL4, the labeled neurons were responsive to sucrose and all fatty acids tested, which ranged from 4C to 10C (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IR56d neurons respond to diverse appetitive stimuli.
source: Thus, IR56d neurons respond to diverse appetitive stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data in Figure 5E showing responses to multiple tastants.

claim: Flies with a deletion of IR56d lacked responses exclusively to medium-chain fatty acids (6C–8C), while responses to short- (4C and 5C) and long-chain fatty acids (9C and 10C) remained intact.
source: Flies with a deletion of IR56d (IR56dGAL4; UAS-GCaMP6.0) lacked responses exclusively to medium-chain fatty acids (6C–8C), while responses to short- (4C and 5C) and long-chain fatty acids (9C and 10C) remained intact (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Inclusion of an IR56d rescue transgene restored the physiological response to medium-chain fatty acids.
source: Consistent with the rescue of behavioral defects, inclusion of an IR56d rescue transgene (IR56dGAL4; UAS-GCaMP6.0/UAS-IR56d) restored the physiological response to medium-chain fatty acids (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: At both behavioral and physiological levels IR56dGAL4 is required for taste responses to medium-chain fatty acids.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that at both behavioral and physiological levels IR56dGAL4 is required for taste responses to medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined behavioral (Figure 4G) and calcium imaging data (Figure 5F-H).

claim: The two populations of IR56d neurons appear to differ in function as the posterior population is responsive to both sucrose and hexanoic acid, while the anterior population is responsive to hexanoic acid, but not sucrose.
source: The two populations appear to differ in function as the posterior population is responsive to both sucrose and hexanoic acid, while the anterior population is responsive to hexanoic acid, but not sucrose (Tauber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by calcium imaging data in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Anterior taste peg neurons were robustly responsive to hexanoic acid (6C), but not by sucrose.
source: In agreement with our previous findings, these neurons were robustly responsive to hexanoic acid (6C), but not by sucrose (Figure 6D–F; Tauber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D-F and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Anterior taste peg neurons responded to other classes of fatty acids including short- (4C and 5C), medium- (7C and 8C) and long-chain (9C and 10C).
source: These neurons also responded to other classes of fatty acids including short- (4C and 5C), medium- (7C and 8C) and long-chain (9C and 10C) (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: The response to short-chain fatty acids was lower in the anterior population compared to the posterior projections.
source: Unlike the posterior projections, which respond similarly to all three classes of fatty acids, the response to short-chain fatty acids was lower in the anterior population.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of calcium imaging data in Figure 5E and Figure 6F.

claim: Differential response between the anterior and posterior populations may provide a mechanism of discrimination between different classes of fatty acids.
source: Therefore, it is possible that differential response between the anterior and posterior populations provides a mechanism of discrimination between different classes of fatty acids.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed differences in responses between anterior and posterior populations.

claim: Medium-chain fatty acids are detected through a shared sensory channel, allowing flies to distinguish medium-chain from short- or long-chain, but not between different medium-chain fatty acids.
source: Taken together, these findings support the notion that medium-chain fatty acids are detected through a shared sensory channel, allowing flies to distinguish medium-chain from short- or long-chain, but not between different medium-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined behavioral and physiological data showing selective IR56d requirement for medium-chain fatty acids and inability to discriminate within this class.

claim: IR56d is selectively involved in responses to medium-chain fatty acids, including 6C, 7C, and 8C fatty acids, and dispensable for responses to shorter and longer-chain fatty acids.
source: Our findings suggest that IR56d is selectively involved in responses to medium-chain fatty acids, including 6C, 7C, and 8C fatty acids, and dispensable for responses to shorter and longer-chain fatty acids.
evidence: This is supported by the combined behavioral and physiological data from Figures 3-5.

claim: Receptor specificity for different classes of fatty acids based on chain length has not been documented in other systems.
source: Such receptor specificity for different classes of fatty acids based on chain length has not been documented in other systems.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to other systems based on general knowledge.

claim: Short- and long-chain fatty acids evoke activity in IR56d-expressing neurons.
source: The finding that short- and long-chain fatty acids also evoke activity in IR56d-expressing neurons posits that additional fatty acid receptors are present in these neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 5E showing responses to all fatty acid classes.

claim: Additional fatty acid receptors are present in IR56d-expressing neurons.
source: The finding that short- and long-chain fatty acids also evoke activity in IR56d-expressing neurons posits that additional fatty acid receptors are present in these neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IR56d neurons respond to short- and long-chain fatty acids even though IR56d is not required for behavioral responses to these fatty acids.

claim: Deletion of Phospholipase C (PLC) signaling selectively impairs fatty acid response while leaving sweet taste intact.
source: Previously, we and others have found that deletion of Phospholipase C (PLC) signaling selectively impairs fatty acid response while leaving sweet taste intact, raising the possibility that activation of distinct intracellular signaling pathways could serve as a mechanism for discrimination between sucrose and fatty acid (Masek and Keene, 2013; Ahn et al., 2017; Tauber et al., 2017), while another suggests TRPA1 and GR64e are targets of PLC and are generally required for fatty acid sensing (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TRPA1 and GR64e are targets of PLC and are generally required for fatty acid sensing.
source: Previously, we and others have found that deletion of Phospholipase C (PLC) signaling selectively impairs fatty acid response while leaving sweet taste intact, raising the possibility that activation of distinct intracellular signaling pathways could serve as a mechanism for discrimination between sucrose and fatty acid (Masek and Keene, 2013; Ahn et al., 2017; Tauber et al., 2017), while another suggests TRPA1 and GR64e are targets of PLC and are generally required for fatty acid sensing (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Flies can discriminate between sugars and fatty acids.
source: Our aversive taste memory assay confirmed previous findings that flies can discriminate between sugars and fatty acids (Tauber et al., 2017), and led to the surprising observation that flies can distinguish between different classes of fatty acids, even though the baseline responsiveness to short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids was similar in innate preference assays.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The baseline responsiveness to short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids was similar in innate preference assays.
source: Our aversive taste memory assay confirmed previous findings that flies can discriminate between sugars and fatty acids (Tauber et al., 2017), and led to the surprising observation that flies can distinguish between different classes of fatty acids, even though the baseline responsiveness to short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids was similar in innate preference assays.
evidence: This is implied by the statement and supported by the PER data in Figure 3C showing similar baseline responses.

claim: Fatty acids are natural by-product of yeast fermentation.
source: Fatty acids are natural by-product of yeast fermentation (Diwan and Gupta, 2018; Nyanga et al., 2013; Oliveira et al., 2011), and their abundance in peaches, for example, declines after ripening (Duan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The abundance of fatty acids in peaches declines after ripening.
source: Fatty acids are natural by-product of yeast fermentation (Diwan and Gupta, 2018; Nyanga et al., 2013; Oliveira et al., 2011), and their abundance in peaches, for example, declines after ripening (Duan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Fatty acids have antifungal activity, which scales with chain length.
source: Further, fatty acids have antifungal activity, which scales with chain length (i.e., the greater the chain length, the greater the antifungal efficiency; Pohl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The ability to discriminate between different classes of fatty acids is likely to be important in determining the stage of fruit ripeness, degree of fermentation, and the general palatability of a potential food source/oviposition site.
source: Thus, the ability to discriminate between different classes of fatty acids is likely to be important in determining the stage of fruit ripeness, degree of fermentation, and the general palatability of a potential food source/oviposition site.
evidence: This is speculated based on the ecological context of fatty acids in fruit fermentation.

claim: Flies were unable to discriminate between different sugars or bitter compounds in a previous study.
source: The finding that flies can distinguish between different classes of fatty acids contrasts with the results of a previous study that applied a similar assay and found that flies were unable to discriminate between different sugars or bitter compounds (Masek and Scott, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fatty acid detection is dependent on IRs, while sweet and bitter tastant detection relies on GRs.
source: One possibility is that this is due to differences in fatty acid detection, which is dependent on IRs, and sweet and bitter tastant detection, which relies on GRs (Chen and Dahanukar, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and general knowledge of taste receptor families.

claim: All types of fatty acids tested increase GR64f neural responsiveness.
source: For example, all types of fatty acids tested increase GR64f neural responsiveness; however, only GR64f neurons are required for PER to medium-chain fatty acids, thereby raising the possibility that short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acid taste discrimination occurs through different neural channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data in Figure 5E showing responses to all fatty acids in IR56d neurons (which co-express GR64f).

claim: Only GR64f neurons are required for PER to medium-chain fatty acids.
source: For example, all types of fatty acids tested increase GR64f neural responsiveness; however, only GR64f neurons are required for PER to medium-chain fatty acids, thereby raising the possibility that short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acid taste discrimination occurs through different neural channels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 3E showing that silencing GR64f neurons reduces PER only to medium-chain fatty acids.

claim: Short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acid taste discrimination may occur through different neural channels.
source: For example, all types of fatty acids tested increase GR64f neural responsiveness; however, only GR64f neurons are required for PER to medium-chain fatty acids, thereby raising the possibility that short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acid taste discrimination occurs through different neural channels.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differential requirement of GR64f neurons for different fatty acid classes.

claim: Flies are able to distinguish between many different odorants, likely due to the complexity of olfactory coding at the level of the receptor as well as in the antennal lobe.
source: Flies are able to distinguish between many different odorants, likely due to the complexity of olfactory coding at the level of the receptor as well as in the antennal lobe (Amin and Lin, 2019; Cognigni et al., 2018; Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Flies can discriminate between odorants sensed by a single olfactory receptor, suggesting that temporal coding also plays a role in discrimination.
source: However, flies can also discriminate between odorants sensed by a single olfactory receptor, suggesting that temporal coding also plays a role in discrimination (DasGupta and Waddell, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Similar mechanisms to olfactory discrimination may underlie discrimination between different classes of fatty acid tastants.
source: It is possible that similar mechanisms underlie discrimination between different classes of fatty acid tastants.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison to olfactory discrimination mechanisms.

claim: The Drosophila genome encodes 66 IRs.
source: The Drosophila genome encodes 66 IRs, which comprise a recently identified family of receptors implicated in taste, olfaction, and temperature sensation (Benton et al., 2009; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IRs are involved in the detection of many different tastants and function as heteromers that confer sensory specificity.
source: IRs are involved in the detection of many different tastants and function as heteromers that confer sensory specificity (Rytz et al., 2013; van Giesen and Garrity, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IR56d likely functions in a complex with IR25a and IR76b, all three of which are required fatty acid taste.
source: While IR56d expression is restricted to a subset of sweet taste neurons, it likely functions in a complex with IR25a and IR76b, all three of which are required fatty acid taste (Ahn et al., 2017; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing that IR25a and IR76b mutants have reduced PER to fatty acids.

claim: IR25a, IR62a, and IR76b have roles in Ca2+ taste.
source: For example, roles for IR25a, IR62a, and IR76b have been described for Ca2+ taste (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The broad degree of co-expression of IRs in the brain and periphery can provide candidates for those involved in detecting short- and long-chain fatty acids.
